sceneHappening: Prophecy and tongues in the assembly: build up the church, and do it in order
summary: Paul says to pursue love and to desire spiritual gifts, especially that they might prophesy. Someone who speaks in a tongue speaks not to people but to God, for no one understands; the one who prophesies speaks to people for their building up, encouragement, and comfort. The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, but the one who prophesies builds up the church, so Paul would rather they prophesied, unless someone interprets. He gives pictures: a flute or harp that makes no clear sound, and a trumpet that gives an uncertain call. So with yourselves: unless you speak words that are understood, you are speaking into the air. He prays and sings with the spirit and with the mind also. In the assembly he would rather speak five words with his mind to instruct others than ten thousand in a tongue. "Brothers, don't be children in thinking, but in evil be babies, and in thinking be mature." If an unbeliever or outsider comes in and everyone speaks in tongues, will they not say you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, the outsider will be convicted and will say, "God is really among you." When they come together, each has a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation; let all be done for building up. Two or three at most should speak in tongues, one at a time, with someone interpreting; if there is no interpreter, let them keep silent in church. Two or three prophets should speak, and the others weigh what is said. The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets, "for God is not a God of confusion but of peace." Then 14:34-35 says women should keep silent in the churches and ask their husbands at home, and Paul closes: desire to prophesy, do not forbid speaking in tongues, "but let all things be done decently and in order."
whySettingMatters: Meetings of the Corinthian church seem to have been lively, with many people contributing, and some of the more dramatic gifts being treated as signs of status. Paul's concern is not to suppress the gifts but to ensure that they serve the whole group. Whether the "tongues" in this chapter are known human languages or ecstatic speech is debated; Paul says they are directed to God and need interpretation, and he never describes them as foreign languages that visitors would understand. The lines in 14:34-35 are among the most discussed in the letter. Some manuscripts place them after verse 40, which has led some scholars to think they were added later; others think Paul is quoting a Corinthian position, or limiting a particular kind of disruption, like asking questions during the weighing of prophecy. Since 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy aloud, the verses are difficult to square with the rest of the letter, and readers differ on how to resolve this. It is a good place to look at what commentaries say. The last line, "decently and in order," frames the whole chapter: freedom in worship is for building others up.

people.note: Speaks in tongues more than all of them, and prefers five words with his mind.
Eager for tongues; told to seek what builds up.
The unbeliever or outsider who comes into the assembly.

questions: Paul says gifts are measured by whether they "build up." How can a church test that?
Why does Paul value the "mind" in worship as well as the spirit?
What might it say about God that Paul describes him as "a God not of confusion but of peace"?
Verses 34 and 35 are debated by careful readers. How can we handle a difficult passage honestly without hiding the difficulty?

words.note: "The one who prophesies speaks to men for building up" (14:1-6, 14:22-39).
"He who speaks in a language speaks not to men but to God" (14:2-27).
"For building up and exhortation and consolation" (14:3-5, 14:12, 14:26).
"I will pray with the spirit... with the mind also" (14:14-19).
"If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound" (14:8).
"God is not a God of confusion" (14:33).
"Let all things be done decently and in order" (14:40).
